nameStory: Summer flounder earned their name because they migrate into shallow coastal waters during the warm summer months, making them much easier to catch from shore and boats. They're also commonly called "fluke," which comes from their flat, unusual body shape that early fishermen thought looked like a lucky accident or "fluke" of nature.
description: Summer flounder are remarkable flatfish that look like they've been completely flattened by a giant pancake press. These masters of disguise lie on sandy or muddy ocean bottoms with both eyes positioned on their left side, scanning for prey above. They can grow quite large, with some reaching over 20 inches long and weighing several pounds. Their diamond-shaped bodies are perfectly adapted for life as ambush predators on the seafloor.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Completely flattened, diamond-shaped body that feels firm and muscular when handled, like a thick, flexible dinner plate with tapered ends

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Both eyes located on the left side of the head, giving them a lopsided appearance that's unmistakable among New England fish

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Top side varies from brown to olive with darker spots and mottled patterns that can change to match surroundings; bottom side is pure white and feels smooth

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth with sharp teeth that extends past the eye, designed for grabbing fish and crabs

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long dorsal and anal fins run almost the entire length of the body, creating a continuous fringe that undulates gracefully

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found buried in sand or mud in shallow coastal waters, often with just their eyes poking up

habitat: Summer flounder inhabit sandy and muddy bottoms in coastal waters throughout New England, from shallow bays and harbors to depths of about 400 feet offshore. They prefer areas with soft sediments where they can easily bury themselves, often near eelgrass beds, around jetties, or along drop-offs where smaller fish and crabs are abundant. During warmer months, they move into very shallow water where anglers can catch them from piers, beaches, and small boats.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin moving from deeper offshore waters into shallow coastal areas as water temperatures rise, becoming more active and easier to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding summer flounder in shallow New England waters, when they're most abundant near shore and actively feeding in bays and harbors.
seasonality.fall: Still common in coastal waters but beginning to move toward deeper areas as temperatures cool, often showing increased feeding activity before migration.
seasonality.winter: Most adults have moved to deeper offshore waters, though some smaller individuals may remain in deeper parts of harbors and bays.

funFact: Summer flounder are born swimming upright like normal fish, but as they grow, one eye literally migrates across their head to join the other eye, and they flip onto their side permanently - it's like nature's own magic trick happening in slow motion over several weeks!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with winter flounder, but summer flounder have their eyes on the LEFT side of their head (think "summer = sinister = left"), while winter flounder have eyes on the right side. Summer flounder also have much larger mouths with more prominent teeth.
contextualKnowledge: The term "fluke" for summer flounder can be confusing since "fluke" also refers to completely different parasitic worms, but in fishing contexts it almost always means summer flounder. This species is also sometimes called "northern fluke" to distinguish it from southern relatives.
compareHints: Summer flounder are larger and more robust than their cousin the fourspot flounder, which has four distinctive dark spots and rarely exceeds 12 inches. Unlike southern flounder (which barely reach New England waters), summer flounder have more variable coloration and can change their pattern more dramatically to match their surroundings.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Summer Flounder, the Fourspot Flounder has more distinct, evenly-spaced spots rather than irregular blotches and mottling.
Compared to its close relative the summer flounder, southern flounders are typically larger with a proportionally bigger mouth and less distinct spotting patterns.
